summary: This standards-track RFC specifies a Kerberos authorization data container that supersedes AD-KDC-ISSUED. It allows several message authentication codes or signatures to protect the contained authorization data, addressing weaknesses in the older container. It updates RFC 4120.

eli5.summary: A sealed envelope is safer with more than one seal. This gives Kerberos tickets a container that can carry several seals to prove the contents are genuine.

subtitle: A Kerberos ticket container that carries several checksums, so both the KDC and services can check the authorization data inside.

tldr.problem: The AD-KDC-ISSUED container in Kerberos lets a service verify that the KDC issued authorization data, but the service knows the key, so the KDC cannot tell whether the service tampered with it when the ticket comes back as evidence.
tldr.mechanism: AD-CAMMAC adds separate verifiers (MACs) over the same authorization data: one the KDC alone can check, one the service can check, and optional ones for trusted services.
tldr.outcome: It supersedes AD-KDC-ISSUED and updates RFC 4120 with ad-type 96 and key usage 64. Servers and KDCs may still ignore it.

today: RFC 7751 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4120. No later RFC obsoletes it or updates it.

sections.title: What the CAMMAC Is
sections.content:
RFC 7751 defines a new Kerberos authorization data container called the CAMMAC (Container Authenticated by Multiple MACs). Its ASN.1 type is AD-CAMMAC, and it supersedes the AD-KDC-ISSUED container from RFC 4120.

The new container lets both the receiving application service and the Key Distribution Center (KDC) check that the contained authorization data is authentic. It can also carry extra verifiers for "trusted services".
sections.eli5: It is a labelled box that goes inside a Kerberos ticket. The box can carry several stamps, so different people can each check it is real.

sections.title: Why AD-KDC-ISSUED Was Not Enough
sections.content:
In RFC 4120, AD-KDC-ISSUED lets a KDC put positive authorization data in a service ticket. The service can verify the KDC issued it, because the checksum uses a key shared between the KDC and the service.

That works when authorization data flows from the KDC to the service. It breaks down for extensions such as Constrained Delegation (S4U2Proxy), where a service presents a previously issued ticket to the KDC as evidence. Because the service knows the checksum key, the KDC cannot detect whether the service changed the container.

The CAMMAC fixes this with several verifiers. The svc-verifier has the same properties as the old checksum. The kdc-verifier uses a key only the KDC knows, so the KDC does not have to recompute authorization data that may include ephemeral information, such as the strength or type of authentication used. The other-verifiers let a lesser-privileged service show a trusted service on the same host that it acts for a client, without further contact with the KDC.
sections.eli5: If the guard and the visitor share the same secret stamp, the visitor could fake a note. Adding a stamp only the guard owns means the guard can spot a fake.

sections.title: The AD-CAMMAC Encoding
sections.content:
Like Kerberos itself, the container is specified in ASN.1 and encoded with DER. The ad-data of the authorization data element is the DER encoding of AD-CAMMAC.

AD-CAMMAC is a sequence of elements (the authorization data being protected), an optional kdc-verifier, an optional svc-verifier and an optional other-verifiers list. A Verifier is a CHOICE with only one alternative today, Verifier-MAC; future extensions might add public-key signatures.

A Verifier-MAC holds an optional identifier (a principal name), an optional kvno, an optional enctype and a required mac, an RFC 3961 checksum. The identifier, key version and encryption type help the recipient find the key. The key usage number for the checksum is 64.
sections.eli5: The box has a list of what is inside and then up to three kinds of stamps. Each stamp says whose key made it and holds the stamp itself.

sections.title: The Three Kinds of Verifier
sections.content:
The kdc-verifier uses a long-term key of the local Ticket-Granting Service. Unlike the others, it is computed over a modified EncTicketPart of the surrounding ticket, in which the authorization data is replaced by the elements of the CAMMAC. This binds it to the rest of the ticket, so a malicious service cannot substitute a mismatched CAMMAC from another ticket.

The svc-verifier uses the same long-term service key that encrypts the ticket. It MUST be present if the ticket's service principal is not the local TGS, including cross-realm TGTs.

The other-verifiers each use a long-term key of the principal named in identifier, which MUST be present and be a valid principal in the realm. A KDC MAY add "trusted service" verifiers. Unless configured otherwise, the KDC SHOULD find that principal by replacing the service component of the ticket's sname with host. The kvno and enctype SHOULD be given.

Applications and KDCs MAY ignore the container. For older implementations, a KDC issuing one SHOULD wrap it in an AD-IF-RELEVANT container unless the application server is likely to recognize it.
sections.eli5: One stamp is for the guard only, one is for the room the ticket opens, and some are for helpers the guard trusts. Each is made with a different secret.

sections.title: Assigned Numbers
sections.content: The RFC updates RFC 4120 in three places. The ad-type number 96 is assigned to AD-CAMMAC. The table of ad-types is updated to map 96 to "DER encoding of AD-CAMMAC". The key usage number 64 is assigned for the Verifier-MAC checksum.
sections.eli5: Every kind of box needs a number so everyone recognizes it. This one gets 96, and its stamps use 64.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A KDC treats a CAMMAC as coming from a local-realm KDC when it verifies the kdc-verifier, or verifies an svc-verifier whose key only local KDCs know, or when no verifiers are present, the ticket key is known only to local KDCs and all local KDCs filter out client-submitted CAMMACs. A KDC MAY omit the kdc-verifier when it is not needed, for example to shrink tickets, if every local KDC filters client-submitted CAMMACs or the service cannot use S4U2Proxy.

Extracting a CAMMAC from its ticket can turn it into a bearer token, and it may not identify the client. The kdc-verifier binds only to the authorization data inside the CAMMAC, not to other data in the ticket; the non-standard AD-SIGNEDPATH type tries to do that, and two such types are very difficult to combine.

The kdc-verifier also does not bind the service principal name. Someone with the keys of two services could move a ticket between them and alter the svc-verifier to match. If an application needs that binding, the KDC MUST include an authorization data element in the CAMMAC that names the service principal.
sections.eli5: A stamp proves the note came from the guard, but a note taken out of its envelope can be used by anyone, so be careful where copies go.

viz.caption: THE THREE VERIFIER FIELDS OF AD-CAMMAC

items.title: kdc-verifier
items.text: Key known only to the KDC; computed over the modified EncTicketPart.

items.title: svc-verifier
items.text: Service key that encrypts the ticket; MUST be present if the service is not the local TGS.

items.title: other-verifiers
items.text: Keys of named trusted-service principals; optional.

data.title: AD-CAMMAC
data.code:
AD-CAMMAC ::= SEQUENCE {
  elements        [0] AuthorizationData,
  kdc-verifier    [1] Verifier-MAC OPTIONAL,
  svc-verifier    [2] Verifier-MAC OPTIONAL,
  other-verifiers [3] SEQUENCE (SIZE (1..MAX))
                      OF Verifier OPTIONAL
}
